claim: The skin consists of two basic layers: the epidermis and the dermis.
source: The skin consists of two basic layers: the epidermis and the dermis.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript describing the basic anatomical structure of the skin.

claim: The epidermis forms the outermost layer and is separated from the underlying dermis by a basement membrane.
source: The epidermis forms the outermost layer, and it is separated from the underlying dermis by a basement membrane.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical description stated in the manuscript.

claim: The epidermis provides protection against pathogens and UV light while preventing excessive water loss.
source: It provides protection against pathogens and UV light, while preventing excessive water loss from the inside.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the functional properties of the epidermis.

claim: The dermis contributes to the mechanical properties of the skin such as elasticity and flexibility due to its high content of collagen and elastin fibers.
source: The dermis contributes to the mechanical properties of the skin, such as elasticity and flexibility, due to its high content of collagen and elastin fibers.
evidence: This is a direct statement linking dermal composition to mechanical properties.

claim: The dermis contains various appendages including sweat and sebaceous glands and hair follicles.
source: It also contains various appendages, including sweat and sebaceous glands and hair follicles, which contribute to physical protection, thermoregulation, sensation, and lubrication of the skin.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical description of dermal structures.

claim: The subcutis or hypodermis consists mainly of adipocytes and connective tissue and connects the skin to the deep fascia.
source: Below the dermis is the subcutis or hypodermis, which consists mainly of adipocytes and connective tissue and connects the skin to the deep fascia.
evidence: This is a direct anatomical description of the subcutis.

claim: Keratinocytes are the most numerous cell type in the epidermis.
source: Keratinocytes are the most numerous cell type in the epidermis, ensuring its physical stability.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cellular composition of the epidermis.

claim: Keratinocytes sense microbial components via Toll-like receptors (TLR), NOD-like receptors (NLRs), and C-type lectin receptors like dectin-1.
source: Beyond this structural role, they also sense microbial components via Toll-like receptors (TLR), NOD-like receptors (NLRs), and C-type lectin receptors like dectin-1, leading to the production of cytokines, such as IL-1β and IL-36. These are important for the antimicrobial and immunological properties of the skin (Goldstein et al., 2020; Klicznik et al., 2018; Pfaff et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three research papers.

claim: Keratinocyte sensing of microbial components leads to the production of cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-36.
source: Beyond this structural role, they also sense microbial components via Toll-like receptors (TLR), NOD-like receptors (NLRs), and C-type lectin receptors like dectin-1, leading to the production of cytokines, such as IL-1β and IL-36. These are important for the antimicrobial and immunological properties of the skin (Goldstein et al., 2020; Klicznik et al., 2018; Pfaff et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three research papers.

claim: The maintenance and renewal of Langerhans cells in steady state relies on IL-34 produced by keratinocytes.
source: As an example, the maintenance and renewal of LCs in steady state relies on IL-34 produced by keratinocytes (Greter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Greter et al., 2012.

claim: Langerhans cells are considered to be long-lived, self-renewing resident macrophages.
source: Although LCs share many characteristics with dendritic cells (DCs), they are considered to be long-lived, self-renewing resident macrophages (Mϕ; Doebel et al., 2017; Mass et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: Langerhans cells derive from embryonic precursors which transmigrate from the dermis and differentiate postnatally into a mature, self-renewing network of interdigitating cells.
source: They derive from embryonic precursors, which transmigrate from the dermis and differentiate postnatally into a mature, self-renewing network of interdigitating cells (Hoeffel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoeffel et al., 2012.

claim: Upon inflammation or injury, monocyte-derived Langerhans cells can infiltrate the niche.
source: However, upon inflammation or injury, 'short-term' monocyte-derived LCs can infiltrate the niche (Merad et al., 2008; Seré et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: The lower epidermal layer in mice, the stratum spinosum, hosts a distinct population of branched γδ T-cells known as dendritic epidermal T-cells (DETC).
source: The lower epidermal layer in mice, the stratum spinosum, hosts a distinct population of branched γẟ T-cells, known as dendritic epidermal T-cells (DETC).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cellular composition of the mouse epidermis.

claim: Dendritic epidermal T-cells sense stress or damage in keratinocytes, aiding in wound healing and skin homeostasis.
source: They sense stress or damage in keratinocytes, aiding in wound healing and skin homeostasis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the function of DETCs.

claim: In humans, most epidermal T-cells are αβ T-cells, particularly a non-circulating resident memory population.
source: In humans, most epidermal T-cells are αβ T-cells, particularly a non-circulating resident memory population, seeding the skin following the resolution of infection and contributing to the long-term tissue surveillance (Ho and Kupper, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ho and Kupper, 2019.

claim: The healthy dermis is inhabited by innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), in particular ILC2, and different T-cell subsets.
source: The healthy dermis is inhabited by innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), in particular ILC2, and different T-cell subsets, that is dermal γẟ T-cells, mucosa-associated invariant T-cells (MAIT), and CD4 + cells (Ho and Kupper, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ho and Kupper, 2019.

claim: The dermis supports mast cells, eosinophils, and numerous DC populations, with conventional CD11b+ DCs being the most prevalent.
source: The dermis also supports mast cells, eosinophils, and numerous DC populations, with conventional CD11b+ DCs being the most prevalent (Belkaid and Tamoutounour, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Belkaid and Tamoutounour, 2016.

claim: Macrophages are the dominant immune cell type in the dermis in terms of absolute numbers.
source: In terms of absolute numbers, Mϕ are the dominant immune cell type in the dermis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the relative abundance of macrophages in the dermis.

claim: Dermal macrophages are a heterogeneous population consisting of multiple subpopulations with distinct lifespans, localizations, and transcriptional profiles.
source: Dermal Mϕ are a heterogeneous population in the adult, consisting of multiple subpopulations with distinct lifespans, localizations, and transcriptional profiles (Tamoutounour et al., 2013, Kolter et al., 2019; Lohrmann et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three research papers.

claim: The dermis is initially seeded by erythro-myeloid progenitors derived from the yolk sac and later the fetal liver.
source: As most tissues, the dermis is initially seeded by erythro-myeloid progenitors derived from the yolk sac and later the fetal liver (Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015.

claim: Embryonic macrophages proliferate locally and persist into adulthood but can be replaced by monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: While these embryonic Mϕ proliferate locally and persist into adulthood, they can also be replaced to tissue-specific extents by monocyte-derived Mϕ derived from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow.
evidence: This is a direct statement about macrophage ontogeny and turnover.

claim: In the dermis, macrophages receive significant input by circulating monocytes, leading to replacement of up to 50% of the population.
source: In the dermis, Mϕ receive a significant input by circulating monocytes, leading to replacement of up to 50% of the population (Kolter et al., 2019; Lohrmann et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: Macrophages with long-term residency have a more immunosuppressive phenotype, while infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophages are more primed towards immune response and inflammation.
source: For example, Mϕ with long-term residency have a more immunosuppressive phenotype, akin to LCs in the epidermis, while infiltrating monocyte-derived Mϕ are more primed towards immune response and inflammation (Lohrmann et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lohrmann et al., 2025.

claim: LYVE-1+ dermal macrophages associated with blood vessels have distinct features and functions compared to long-lived CX3CR1hi sensory nerve-associated macrophages.
source: Moreover, LYVE-1+ dermal Mϕ associated with blood vessels have distinct features and functions compared to, for example, long-lived CX3CR1hi sensory nerve-associated Mϕ, which are differentially imprinted by their TGF-β-rich environment (Chakarov et al., 2019; Kolter et al., 2019; Kolter et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three research papers.

claim: The density of the resident macrophage network in the skin is strictly regulated at the site.
source: Interestingly, the density of the resident Mϕ network in the skin is strictly regulated at the site, as demonstrated in Irf8-/- mice, which exhibit a complete lack of circulating monocytes, yet show the same Mϕ density and diversity of transcriptional states as wild-type mice (Lohrmann et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lohrmann et al., 2025 and experimental data from Irf8-/- mice.

claim: Macrophages are essential for maintaining skin barrier integrity and repair in response to infection or injury.
source: In response to infection or injury, Mϕ are essential for maintaining skin barrier integrity and repair (Barreiro et al., 2016; Kolter et al., 2019; Shook et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three research papers.

claim: Infections often lead to depletion of the resident macrophage pool, followed by replacement with infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: However, infections often lead to depletion of the resident Mϕ pool, followed by a replacement with infiltrating monocyte-derived Mϕ (Forde et al., 2023; Ginhoux et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: Trained immunity is a process by which innate immune cells that previously encountered a pathogenic stimulus show an enhanced and more rapid response to a subsequent pathogenic challenge.
source: Trained immunity (TI) or innate immune memory is a process by which innate immune cells, which previously encountered a pathogenic stimulus, show an enhanced and more rapid response to a subsequent pathogenic challenge.
evidence: This is a direct definition of trained immunity provided in the manuscript.

claim: The primed response pattern in trained immunity is characterized by enhanced formation of cytokines, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and increased phagocytosis.
source: This primed response pattern is characterized by enhanced formation of cytokines, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and increased phagocytosis (Netea et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Netea et al., 2011.

claim: Trained immunity can last from weeks to several years but is generally shorter than adaptive immune memory.
source: TI can last from weeks to several years, but it is generally shorter than adaptive immune memory (Netea et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Netea et al., 2020.

claim: BCG and β-glucan were most frequently used as experimental inducers of trained immunity.
source: While the tuberculosis vaccine Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) and the fungal cell wall component β-glucan were most frequently used as experimental inducers of TI, other triggers have been identified, for example oxidized low-density lipoproteins and S. aureus (Bekkering et al., 2014; Carlile et al., 2024; Feuerstein et al., 2020; Kaufmann et al., 2018; Moorlag et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement about commonly used experimental inducers, supported by citations.

claim: Oxidized low-density lipoproteins and S. aureus have been identified as triggers of trained immunity.
source: While the tuberculosis vaccine Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) and the fungal cell wall component β-glucan were most frequently used as experimental inducers of TI, other triggers have been identified, for example oxidized low-density lipoproteins and S. aureus (Bekkering et al., 2014; Carlile et al., 2024; Feuerstein et al., 2020; Kaufmann et al., 2018; Moorlag et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to five research papers.

claim: BCG vaccination protects against Candida albicans in severe combined immunodeficient (SCID) mice.
source: One important example of heterologous TI is the protective effect of BCG vaccination against Candida albicans in severe combined immunodeficient (SCID) mice (Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2012; van 't van 't Wout et al., 1992), which lack functional T- and B- cells, highlighting the critical role of innate immune cells in memory responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: The protective effect of BCG vaccination against Candida albicans in SCID mice highlights the critical role of innate immune cells in memory responses.
source: One important example of heterologous TI is the protective effect of BCG vaccination against Candida albicans in severe combined immunodeficient (SCID) mice (Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2012; van 't van 't Wout et al., 1992), which lack functional T- and B- cells, highlighting the critical role of innate immune cells in memory responses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation in SCID mice, which lack adaptive immune cells.

claim: High glycolytic activity and byproducts of the tricarboxylic acid cycle can modulate enzymes which mediate histone modification.
source: For example, in infections, high glycolytic activity and byproducts of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (e.g. fumarate) can modulate enzymes which mediate histone modification, thereby altering chromatin accessibility and the transcription of inflammatory genes (Figure 1; Arts et al., 2016; Riksen and Netea, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: S. aureus is a skin colonizer in around 30% of humans.
source: S. aureus is a skin colonizer in around 30% of humans (Eriksen et al., 1995; Kluytmans and Wertheim, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: S. aureus is the leading cause of skin and skin structure infections.
source: However, barrier disruption or immune dysregulation can enable opportunistic pathogenicity, making S. aureus the leading cause of skin and skin structure infections.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the clinical significance of S. aureus.

claim: S. aureus evades host immunity via inhibition of phagocytosis, degradation of antimicrobial peptides, and neutrophil-targeted toxin production.
source: S. aureus uses a multitude of means to evade host immunity, e.g., via inhibition of phagocytosis, degradation of antimicrobial peptides, and neutrophil-targeted toxin production (Thammavongsa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thammavongsa et al., 2015.

claim: Patients with MyD88 or IRAK4 deficiencies experience recurrent S. aureus infections.
source: Patients with MyD88 or interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 4 (IRAK4) deficiencies experience recurrent S. aureus infections, which underscores the critical role of TLR and IL1R recognition by innate immune cells in generating an effective inflammatory response against the bacterium (Picard et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Picard et al., 2010.

claim: Macrophages completely fail to respond to whole streptococci and staphylococci in MyD88/IRAK4 deficiency.
source: Mϕs play a particularly important role, as they completely fail to respond to whole streptococci and staphylococci in MyD88/IRAK4 deficiency, while circulating monocytes still mount a residual inflammatory response (Craig-Mueller et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Craig-Mueller et al., 2020.

claim: MyD88 in macrophages is critical for abscess resolution in staphylococcal skin infection.
source: In addition, MyD88 in Mϕ has been shown to be critical for abscess resolution in staphylococcal skin infection (Feuerstein et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feuerstein et al., 2015.

claim: IL-1β-IL1R signaling is critical for bacterial clearance and wound healing in staphylococcal skin infection.
source: In this context, IL-1β-IL1R signaling has been demonstrated to be critical not only for bacterial clearance but also for wound healing.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the role of IL-1β signaling.

claim: Neutrophils are a primary source of IL-1β in staphylococcal skin infection.
source: In staphylococcal skin infection, neutrophils are a primary source of IL-1β, and IL-1β deficiency impairs bacterial clearing and abscess formation (Cho et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2012.

claim: IL-1β deficiency impairs bacterial clearing and abscess formation in staphylococcal skin infection.
source: In staphylococcal skin infection, neutrophils are a primary source of IL-1β, and IL-1β deficiency impairs bacterial clearing and abscess formation (Cho et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2012.

claim: S. aureus sensing leading to IL-1β production and signaling through MyD88 in keratinocytes boosts skin regeneration after injury.
source: S. aureus sensing leading to IL-1β production and signaling through MyD88 in keratinocytes has also been shown to boost skin regeneration after injury (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: IL-17A is crucial for protection against S. aureus skin infections.
source: Another cytokine that is crucial for protection against S. aureus skin infections is IL-17A.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the role of IL-17A.

claim: Patients with hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) resulting from mutations in STAT3 experience recurrent S. aureus skin infections due to a defective Th17 response.
source: Its importance is evident in patients with hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES), resulting from mutations in STAT3. Affected humans experience recurrent S. aureus skin infections due to a defective Th17 response (Miller and Cho, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miller and Cho, 2011.

claim: Neutrophils from HIES patients are more sensitive to lytic cell death in S. aureus infection and have a shorter half-life.
source: Although neutrophils from HIES patients appear to be functional in chemotaxis and ROS production, they are more sensitive to lytic cell death in S. aureus infection and have a shorter half-life (Farmand et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Farmand et al., 2018.

claim: Mice deficient in IL-17 signaling spontaneously develop S. aureus infections.
source: Moreover, mice deficient in IL-17 signaling spontaneously develop S. aureus infections (Cho et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cho et al., 2010.

claim: S. aureus skin infections induce local hypoxia, leading to induction of HIF-1α and ultimately IL-1β production in keratinocytes and dermal macrophages.
source: In addition, S. aureus skin infections induce local hypoxia, leading to induction of the hypoxia-inducible factor 1 a (HIF-1α) and ultimately IL-1β production, both in keratinocytes (Wickersham et al., 2017) and dermal Mϕ (Forde et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: Macrophages increase levels of the TCA metabolite succinate under inflammation, which stabilizes HIF-1α.
source: Mechanistically, Mϕ increase levels of the TCA metabolite succinate under inflammation, which stabilizes HIF-1α (Tannahill et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tannahill et al., 2013.

claim: HIF-1α induces expression of glycolytic genes, which promote a switch from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis and the upregulation of Il-1β in macrophages.
source: HIF-1α, in turn, induces expression of glycolytic genes, which promote a switch from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis and the upregulation of Il-1β in Mϕ (Woods et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Woods et al., 2022.

claim: At 1 day post-infection, dermal macrophages can bypass the need for HIF-1α by initiating a metabolic shift and generating an effective inflammatory response in a GM-CSF-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, however, at 1 day post-infection (dpi), dermal Mϕ can bypass the need for HIF-1α by initiating a metabolic shift and generating an effective inflammatory response in a GM-CSF-dependent manner (Forde et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Forde et al., 2023.

claim: In the infected dermis at 1 dpi, γδ T-cells produce GM-CSF, triggering metabolic rewiring in both resident and newly recruited macrophages.
source: However, in the infected dermis at 1 dpi, γδ T-cells produce GM-CSF, triggering metabolic rewiring in both resident and newly recruited Mϕ.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the source and effects of GM-CSF during infection.

claim: GM-CSF induces the production of itaconate, a metabolite that is critical for the timely resolution of infection.
source: GM-CSF also induces the production of itaconate, a metabolite that is critical for the timely resolution of infection (Forde et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Forde et al., 2023.

claim: Mice previously infected subcutaneously with methicillin-resistant S. aureus exhibit increased efficiency in early bacterial clearance in a subsequent infection, independently of T- and B- cells.
source: Mice previously infected subcutaneously with methicillin-resistant S. aureus exhibit increased efficiency in early bacterial clearance in a subsequent infection, independently of T- and B- cells (Chan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2017.

claim: Skin lesions of primed mice showed increased neutrophils, macrophages, Langerin-positive DCs, and NK cells compared to naive controls.
source: In this model, skin lesions of primed mice showed increased neutrophils, Mϕ, Langerin-positive DCs, and NK cells compared to naive controls, as well as elevated IL-17A, IL-22, and IFN-γ levels.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations in primed mice.

claim: In Rag1-/- mice, IL-22 levels were higher compared to naïve mice after S. aureus infection, confirming an innate source.
source: Notably, in Rag1-/- mice, which lack functional T- and B- cells, IL-22 levels were higher compared to naïve mice, confirming an innate source (Chan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2017 and experimental data from Rag1-/- mice.

claim: Elevated IL-17, IL-6, CXCL9, and CCL5 levels were observed in the skin after re-infection with S. aureus.
source: In a follow-up study, elevated IL-17, IL-6, CXCL9, and CCL5 levels were observed in the skin after re-infection.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations in a follow-up study.

claim: Bone marrow-derived macrophages of previously infected mice displayed enhanced S. aureus killing in vitro.
source: Bone marrow-derived Mϕ (BMDM) of previously infected mice displayed enhanced S. aureus killing in vitro and conferred protection when adoptively transferred into a flank of naïve mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations.

claim: Bone marrow-derived macrophages from previously infected mice conferred protection when adoptively transferred into naïve mice.
source: Bone marrow-derived Mϕ (BMDM) of previously infected mice displayed enhanced S. aureus killing in vitro and conferred protection when adoptively transferred into a flank of naïve mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations.

claim: The training effect in bone marrow-derived macrophages persisted even after in vitro differentiation for two weeks, pointing to hematopoietic stem cells undergoing immune training.
source: As the effect persisted even after in vitro differentiation of BMDM for two weeks, these findings pointed to hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) undergoing immune training in S. aureus infection, leading to a long-term memory phenomenon (Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations, supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2018.

claim: β-glucan administration or BCG vaccination can train HSCs in the bone marrow, which enhances myelopoiesis and induces the generation of trained progeny.
source: Indeed, pivotal studies revealed that β-glucan administration or BCG vaccination can train HSCs in the bone marrow, which enhances myelopoiesis and induces the generation of trained progeny, for example monocytes and Mϕ, and thus improves antimycobacterial immunity (Bekkering et al., 2014; Cirovic et al., 2020; Kaufmann et al., 2018; Mitroulis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four research papers.

claim: A strictly localized intradermal S. aureus infection induced a local trained immunity response mediated by resident dermal macrophages.
source: In contrast, a strictly localized intradermal S. aureus infection, which avoids systemic dissemination, induced a local TI response mediated by the resident dermal Mϕ (Feuerstein et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feuerstein et al., 2020.

claim: Local trained immunity protection is independent of T-, B-, and NK-cells and is associated with upregulation of STAT1 and CXCL9 in resident dermal macrophages.
source: This protection is independent of T-, B-, and NK-cells and is associated with upregulation of STAT1 and CXCL9 in bona fide resident dermal Mϕ.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the characteristics of local trained immunity.

claim: Trained immunity in dermal macrophages during S. aureus infection appears to be at least partially independent of MyD88 signaling.
source: Furthermore, although β-glucan-initiated immune memory has been shown to cause histone trimethylation at H3K4 engaging promoter sites of Myd88 in monocytes (Quintin et al., 2012), TI in dermal Mϕ during S. aureus infection appears to be at least partially independent of MyD88 signaling (Feuerstein et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: Prolonged GM-CSF production after primary staphylococcal infection is required for improved clearance of a secondary infection and acquisition of trained immunity.
source: Importantly, prolonged GM-CSF production after primary staphylococcal infection is required for improved clearance of a secondary infection and thus for the acquisition of TI (Forde et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Forde et al., 2023.

claim: Macrophages exhibit a type I interferon signature at the stage when S. aureus infection is largely cleared.
source: Next to the GM-CSF phenotype, Mϕ also exhibit a type I interferon (IFN) signature in Mϕ at the stage when S. aureus infection is largely cleared (Forde et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Forde et al., 2023.

claim: Interferons (both type I and type II) have been identified as important for the development of trained immunity in bone marrow stem cells and macrophages in the lung.
source: Interferons (IFNs), both type I and type II, have been identified as important for the development of TI in bone marrow stem cells (Kaufmann et al., 2018) and Mϕ in the lung (Zahalka et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: The memory response in dermal macrophages could be prolonged in Ccr2-/- mice, in which macrophage replacement is delayed due to significantly reduced monocyte influx.
source: Indeed, the memory response could be prolonged in Ccr2-/- mice, in which Mϕ replacement is delayed due to significantly reduced monocyte influx (Feuerstein et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feuerstein et al., 2020 and experimental data from Ccr2-/- mice.

claim: For long-lasting trained immunity in barrier tissues, priming must occur at the HSCs and myeloid precursor level.
source: These findings suggest that for long-lasting TI in barrier tissues, priming must occur at the HSCs and myeloid precursor level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about macrophage turnover and memory duration.

claim: Glycolysis has been shown to be essential for trained immunity in monocytes.
source: Glycolysis has been shown to be essential for TI in monocytes (Cheng et al., 2014), and polymorphisms in glycolytic genes (e.g. HK, PFKP) reduce the production of TNF and IL-6 after re-stimulation (Arts et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: Polymorphisms in glycolytic genes reduce the production of TNF and IL-6 after re-stimulation.
source: Glycolysis has been shown to be essential for TI in monocytes (Cheng et al., 2014), and polymorphisms in glycolytic genes (e.g. HK, PFKP) reduce the production of TNF and IL-6 after re-stimulation (Arts et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arts et al., 2018a.

claim: In trained monocytes, glycolysis feeds the pentose phosphate pathway, which supports the production of nucleotides and NADPH.
source: In trained monocytes, glycolysis feeds the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), which supports the production of nucleotides and NADPH (Arts et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arts et al., 2016.

claim: Immune training is attenuated when cholesterol synthesis, fatty acid oxidation, or glutaminolysis are blocked.
source: In addition, immune training is attenuated when cholesterol synthesis, fatty acid oxidation, or glutaminolysis are blocked (Arts et al., 2016; Zahalka et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: Glutaminolysis leads to an accumulation of α-ketoglutarate and fumarate, which enhances epigenetic memory by inhibiting KDM5 demethylases.
source: As an example, glutaminolysis leads to an accumulation of α-ketoglutarate and fumarate, which enhances epigenetic memory by inhibiting KDM5 demethylases responsible for demethylating histone H3K4 (Arts et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arts et al., 2016.

claim: Histone modifications are rapidly induced by an inflammatory stimulus and are only partially reversed when the cell returns to a resting state.
source: In principle, histone modifications are rapidly induced by an inflammatory stimulus and are only partially reversed when the cell returns to a resting state.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dynamics of histone modifications.

claim: Residual histone marking facilitates chromatin accessibility and faster transcription of inflammatory mediators in response to subsequent challenges.
source: This residual marking facilitates chromatin accessibility and therefore faster transcription of inflammatory mediators in response to subsequent challenges.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the functional consequence of residual histone modifications.

claim: Inhibition of demethylases and deacetylases or activation of lysine methyl-transferase by metabolites directly connects metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming in innate memory.
source: Inhibition of demethylases and deacetylases or activation of lysine methyl-transferase by metabolites therefore directly connects metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming in innate memory (Bekkering et al., 2014; Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2012; Mitroulis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three research papers.

claim: S. aureus-derived lactate inhibits histone deacetylase 11 (HDAC11), leading to upregulated HDAC6 activity and increased acetylation of histone 3 at the Il-10 promoter in macrophages.
source: For example, S. aureus-derived lactate inhibits the histone deacetylase 11 (HDAC11), leading to upregulated HDAC6 activity and increased acetylation of histone 3 at the Il-10 promoter in Mϕ (Heim et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heim et al., 2020.

claim: Re-infection with the ΔhemB S. aureus strain led to local fumarate reduction in the skin and inhibited the development of trained immunity.
source: The importance of host-pathogen interactions and competition for nutrients was illustrated using the ΔhemB S. aureus strain, which relies solely on glycolysis. Re-infection with the ΔhemB strain led to local fumarate reduction in the skin and ultimately inhibited the development of TI (Wong Fok Lung et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wong Fok Lung et al., 2020.

claim: Specific S. aureus variants isolated from chronically colonized patients had polymorphisms in genes associated with enhanced glycolysis and limitation of fumarate generation.
source: Moreover, specific S. aureus variants isolated from the skin of chronically colonized patients had polymorphisms in genes associated with enhanced glycolysis and limitation of fumarate generation, and one of these strains led to a decrease in innate memory as compared to the prevalent USA300 strain (Acker et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Acker et al., 2019.

claim: Mice exposed to S. aureus or heat-fixed C. albicans develop trained immunity, but enhanced immune responses paradoxically boost persistence of antibiotic-resistant S. aureus.
source: Interestingly, a recent study revealed that although mice exposed to S. aureus or heat-fixed C. albicans develop trained immunity, enhanced immune responses paradoxically boost persistence of antibiotic-resistant S. aureus (Lin et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2024.

claim: The paradoxical boost in antibiotic-resistant S. aureus persistence was specifically attributed to the accumulation of sodium fumarate.
source: This phenomenon was specifically attributed to the accumulation of sodium fumarate (independently of other fumarate derivatives) and could be reversed by the administration of an antidiabetic drug metformin, which acts as an mTOR inhibitor and trained immunity suppressor (Lin et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2024.

claim: Metformin can reverse the paradoxical boost in antibiotic-resistant S. aureus persistence by acting as an mTOR inhibitor and trained immunity suppressor.
source: This phenomenon was specifically attributed to the accumulation of sodium fumarate (independently of other fumarate derivatives) and could be reversed by the administration of an antidiabetic drug metformin, which acts as an mTOR inhibitor and trained immunity suppressor (Lin et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2024.

claim: Epicutaneous S. aureus infection triggers epigenetic and metabolic reprograming of eosinophil progenitors in the bone marrow.
source: A recent study demonstrated that epicutaneous S. aureus infection triggers epigenetic and metabolic reprograming of the eosinophil progenitors in the bone marrow, leading to an enhanced subsequent allergic sensitization both at the site of infection (skin) and also in a distal site (lung) (Radhouani et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Radhouani et al., 2025.

claim: Epicutaneous S. aureus infection leads to enhanced subsequent allergic sensitization both at the site of infection (skin) and in a distal site (lung).
source: A recent study demonstrated that epicutaneous S. aureus infection triggers epigenetic and metabolic reprograming of the eosinophil progenitors in the bone marrow, leading to an enhanced subsequent allergic sensitization both at the site of infection (skin) and also in a distal site (lung) (Radhouani et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Radhouani et al., 2025.

claim: The effect of epicutaneous S. aureus infection on eosinophils was transferable by bone marrow transplantation and was driven by soluble mediators such as IL-33.
source: This effect was transferable by bone marrow transplantation and was driven by soluble mediators, for example IL-33.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations.

claim: Eosinophils lacking the IL-33 receptor exhibited impaired bone marrow expansion post-infection and reduced lung infiltration upon allergen inhalation.
source: In particular, eosinophils lacking the IL-33 receptor exhibited impaired bone marrow expansion post-infection and a reduced lung infiltration upon allergen inhalation (Radhouani et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Radhouani et al., 2025.

claim: Neutrophils acquire memory-like properties primarily through alterations in their bone marrow progenitors rather than through changes in their terminally differentiated state.
source: Similarly, neutrophils appear to acquire memory-like properties primarily through alterations in their bone marrow progenitors, rather than through changes in their terminally differentiated state (Moorlag et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moorlag et al., 2020.

claim: After intradermal BCG vaccination, neutrophils displayed changes for 90 days post vaccination, including increased activation markers and enhanced antimicrobial functions.
source: After intradermal BCG vaccination of healthy volunteers, neutrophils displayed changes for 90 days post vaccination, such as increased activation markers (CD11b, CD66b), and enhanced antimicrobial functions (degranulation, phagocytosis, ROS production) upon secondary stimulation ex vivo.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations in human volunteers.

claim: Changes in neutrophils after BCG vaccination were associated with sustained epigenetic modifications, such as increased H3K4me3 at promoters of genes involved in inflammation and metabolism.
source: These changes were associated with sustained epigenetic modifications, such as increased H3K4me3 at promoters of genes involved in inflammation (e.g. STAT4) and metabolism (e.g. mTOR and PFKP; Moorlag et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moorlag et al., 2020.

claim: BCG can persist for months in tissue niches like the skin and potentially the bone marrow.
source: Furthermore, BCG can persist for months in tissue niches like the skin, and potentially the bone marrow, making the distinction between TI and effects associated with chronic infection difficult (Hoft et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoft et al., 1999.

claim: An adjuvant derived from cholera toxin (CTB) activates DCs in the skin, promoting long-term maintenance of CD4 T cells, particularly Th17 and Th1 subsets.
source: For example, Antonio-Herrera and colleagues have shown that an adjuvant derived from cholera toxin (CTB) activates DCs in the skin, promoting long-term maintenance of CD4 T cells, in particular Th17 and Th1 subsets (Antonio-Herrera et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Antonio-Herrera et al., 2018.

claim: CTB can directly induce trained immunity in DCs, characterized by higher TNF production, CD86, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) expression upon re-stimulation.
source: In a subsequent study, the same group showed that CTB can directly induce TI in DCs, characterized by higher TNF production, CD86, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) expression upon re-stimulation (Tepale-Segura et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tepale-Segura et al., 2024.

claim: The trained phenotype in DCs was observed both locally in the skin and systemically in bone marrow DC precursors.
source: Importantly, this trained phenotype was observed both locally in the skin and systemically in bone marrow DC precursors (Tepale-Segura et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tepale-Segura et al., 2024.

claim: Immune memory of DCs was shown to be dependent on histone methylation.
source: Notably, immune memory of DCs was shown to be dependent on histone methylation, as demonstrated in vitro in DCs isolated from mice immunized using a specific C. neoformans strain. In this context, DCs were able to produce higher levels of IL-2, IFN-γ, IL-4, and TNF upon secondary challenge (Hole et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hole et al., 2019.

claim: Infection with human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) promotes the induction and long-term maintenance of expanded NK cell populations.
source: One of the first reports on TI identified NK cells with a memory phenotype after cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (Sun et al., 2009). Infection with human CMV (HCMV) promotes the induction and long-term maintenance of expanded NK cell populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2009.

claim: Innate IFN-γ–producing NK cells mediate rapid but short-lived protection after HCMV infection.
source: Resulting innate IFN-γ–producing NK cells mediate rapid but short-lived protection (Luetke-Eversloh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Luetke-Eversloh et al., 2014.

claim: The mechanism of trained immunity in NK cells after HCMV infection is mediated by pro-inflammatory cytokines, which induce demethylation of DNA at loci encoding antiviral cytokines such as IFN-γ.
source: In this context, the underlying mechanism of TI is mediated by pro-inflammatory cytokines, which induce demethylation of DNA at loci encoding antiviral cytokines such as IFN-γ. This cytokine-driven epigenetic remodeling of chromatin was seen to enhance the accessibility of these genes, thereby promoting increased IFN-γ production upon subsequent stimulation (Luetke-Eversloh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Luetke-Eversloh et al., 2014.

claim: In vitro stimulation of NK cells isolated from BCG-vaccinated mice with S. aureus resulted in enhanced and sustained production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IFN-γ.
source: Similarly, in vitro stimulation of NK cells isolated from BCG-vaccinated mice with S. aureus resulted in enhanced and sustained production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IFN-γ (Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2014.

claim: NK cells are not typical constituents of healthy skin.
source: Although NK cells are not typical constituents of a healthy skin (Torcellan et al., 2024), in conditions like atopic dermatitis, they can home to the skin and initiate a cytotoxic response (de Lima et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: In conditions like atopic dermatitis, NK cells can home to the skin and initiate a cytotoxic response.
source: Although NK cells are not typical constituents of a healthy skin (Torcellan et al., 2024), in conditions like atopic dermatitis, they can home to the skin and initiate a cytotoxic response (de Lima et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to de Lima et al., 2024.

claim: The bactericidal properties of NK cells rely on HIF-1α.
source: The bactericidal properties of NK cells rely on HIF-1α, as mice lacking HIF-1α in NKp46+ cells fail to control wound healing and bacterial dissemination in S. aureus and group A streptococcal skin infection (Sobecki et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sobecki et al., 2021.

claim: NK cells can differentiate into long-lived, resident memory-like cells with increased immune responses after secondary exposure to vaccinia virus or S. aureus.
source: Following infection, Torcellan and colleagues elucidated the capacity of NK cells to differentiate into long-lived, resident memory-like cells, with increased immune responses after secondary exposure to either vaccinia virus or S. aureus. Thus, differentiated tissue-resident NK (trNK) cells can rapidly transform into effector NK cells, exhibiting an enhanced immune response (Torcellan et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Torcellan et al., 2024.

claim: Epithelial stem cells (EpSCs) in the basal layer of the epithelium are self-renewing cells maintaining the epithelial tissues of the skin, gastrointestinal lining, and respiratory tract.
source: Epithelial stem cells (EpSCs) in the basal layer of the epithelium are self-renewing cells maintaining the epithelial tissues of the skin, the gastrointestinal lining, and the respiratory tract (Blanpain et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blanpain et al., 2004.

claim: Skin inflammation induces long-lasting memory in epithelial stem cells, enabling faster wound closure upon subsequent injury.
source: Naik et al. found that skin inflammation induces long-lasting memory in EpSCs, enabling faster wound closure upon subsequent injury. This process relies on AIM2, as Aim2-deficient mice show impaired wound healing post-inflammation (Naik et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Naik et al., 2017.

claim: Aim2-deficient mice show impaired wound healing post-inflammation.
source: Naik et al. found that skin inflammation induces long-lasting memory in EpSCs, enabling faster wound closure upon subsequent injury. This process relies on AIM2, as Aim2-deficient mice show impaired wound healing post-inflammation (Naik et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Naik et al., 2017.

claim: Following an initial inflammatory event, primed epithelial stem cells showed increased chromatin accessibility of stress-response genes.
source: Following an initial inflammatory event, primed EpSCs showed increased chromatin accessibility of stress-response genes, allowing for rapid transcriptional activation after a secondary challenge.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations.

claim: Epithelial stem cell memory was localized and not transmittable through circulation to naïve sites and was independent of macrophages, T- and B-cells.
source: EpCS memory was localized and not transmittable through circulation to naïve sites and was independent of Mϕ, T- and B-cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the characteristics of EpSC memory.

claim: The memory of epithelial stem cells was sustained for at least 180 days.
source: The memory of EpSC was sustained for at least 180 days, likely due to their long lifespan and self-renewal capacities (Naik et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Naik et al., 2017.

claim: In vitiligo, IFNγ-responsive fibroblasts were identified as key players in the recruitment and activation of auto-reactive CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells through the secretion of cytokines.
source: For example, in vitiligo, IFNγ-responsive fibroblasts were identified as key players in the recruitment and activation of auto-reactive CD8 +cytotoxic T-cells through the secretion of cytokines, ultimately leading to the loss of melanocytes (Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2022.

claim: In the synovium of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, a fibroblast subpopulation has been implicated in disease promotion via the formation of cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases.
source: In the synovium of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, a fibroblast subpopulation has been implicated in disease promotion via the formation of cytokines and matrix metalloproteinases (Mizoguchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mizoguchi et al., 2018.

claim: The mode of delivery impacts the composition of the early-life skin microbiota.
source: The mode of delivery has been found to impact the composition of the early-life skin microbiota. While infants born vaginally have Lactobacillus as the predominant microbial constituent, those delivered by cesarean section carry more skin-associated bacteria, such as Staphylococcus and Corynebacterium species, with an overall lower microbial diversity (Dominguez-Bello et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: Infants born vaginally have Lactobacillus as the predominant microbial constituent.
source: The mode of delivery has been found to impact the composition of the early-life skin microbiota. While infants born vaginally have Lactobacillus as the predominant microbial constituent, those delivered by cesarean section carry more skin-associated bacteria, such as Staphylococcus and Corynebacterium species, with an overall lower microbial diversity (Dominguez-Bello et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: Infants delivered by cesarean section carry more skin-associated bacteria with an overall lower microbial diversity.
source: The mode of delivery has been found to impact the composition of the early-life skin microbiota. evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: As individuals mature, the skin microbiota undergoes substantial changes, including a decline in Staphylococcus and Streptococcus, greater site-specific specialization, and an increase in lipophilic organisms.
source: As individuals mature, the skin microbiota undergoes substantial changes, including a decline in Staphylococcus and Streptococcus, greater site-specific specialization, and an increase in lipophilic organisms, such as Cutibacterium and Corynebacterium spp. (Luna, 2020; Oh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two research papers.

claim: The microbiota serves as a continuous source of effector molecules that can diffuse across the epidermis to dermis and superficial adipose tissue, engaging pattern recognition receptors.
source: The microbiota serves as a continuous source of effector molecules (e.g. bacterial DNA and rRNA) that can diffuse across the epidermis to dermis and superficial adipose tissue, engaging pattern recognition receptors (PRRs; Nakatsuji et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nakatsuji et al., 2013.

claim: Skin colonization with commensal bacteria promoted tolerance and led to accumulation of Tregs in the neonatal period, an effect not recapitulated in adult mice.
source: For example, skin colonization with commensal bacteria promoted tolerance and led to accumulation of Tregs in the neonatal period, an effect not recapitulated in adult mice, highlighting the importance of exposure to microbiota early in life (Scharschmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scharschmidt et al., 2015.

claim: Microbiota disruption by antibiotic treatment ameliorated psoriasis in adult mice but led to disease exacerbation in neonatal mice.
source: Furthermore, microbiota disruption by antibiotic treatment ameliorated psoriasis in adult mice, but led to disease exacerbation in neonatal mice (Zanvit et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zanvit et al., 2015.

claim: Cutibacterium acnes produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which act as histone deacetylase inhibitors in keratinocytes.
source: Cutibacterium acnes colonizes the lipid-rich, hypoxic environment of the hair follicle where it produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which act as histone deacetylase inhibitors in keratinocytes (Sanford et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sanford et al., 2016.

claim: Short-chain fatty acids from Cutibacterium acnes can shift keratinocytes from a tolerogenic to an inflammatory phenotype.
source: This epigenetic change can shift keratinocytes from a tolerogenic to an inflammatory phenotype, illustrating a direct effect of microbial metabolites on immune response modulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation about SCFAs acting as histone deacetylase inhibitors.

claim: Colonization by Staphylococcus epidermidis can activate dermal DCs and promote IL-17A-mediated T cell responses.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Naik et al., 2015.

claim: BCG vaccination induces memory in alveolar macrophages independently of circulating monocytes and alters the intestinal microbiome and systemic metabolites.
source: There is, however, evidence that the interplay between microbiota and TI might be bi-directional. claim: The microbiota plays a critical role in myelopoiesis, as germ-free and antibiotic-treated mice have reduced numbers of myeloid cell progenitors in bone marrow.

claim: BCG has been used for a long time as a treatment for melanoma by direct intradermal or subcutaneous administration into metastatic lesions.

claim: Tumor-associated macrophages are a major contributor to the melanoma environment, with their inflammatory phenotype being linked to a better prognosis.

claim: Inhibition of HIF-1α alleviated inflammatory symptoms in inflammatory skin conditions.

claim: In patients with vitiligo, an enhanced inflammatory response was found both in circulating monocytes and in structural cells in the skin such as keratinocytes or fibroblasts.

claim: UV radiation induces DNA damage, leading to PRR activation and production of type I interferons, antimicrobial peptides, and cytokines.
